m6-t1.introduction: Read RAG as a defined policy, not a mood. Compare baseline and forecast, weight accepted work honestly and make the decision request impossible to miss.

sections.title: Separate the status dimensions
sections.explanation: A colour means something only when its threshold, cut-off and owner are clear. A schedule dimension can be amber while a mandatory quality issue is red. Do not average away the defect to produce a more comfortable single colour.

items.label: Schedule: amber under this policy
items.detail: A two-working-day forecast delay fits the example’s pre-agreed one-to-three-day amber band.

items.label: Quality: red if mandatory failure
items.detail: A critical unresolved security or allocation failure needs its own explicit status.

items.label: Context: defined and versioned
items.detail: Cut-off, baseline version, owner and thresholds accompany the summary.

sections.caption: Illustrative RAG policy from the lesson. Colours are shown as words and are not universal institutional thresholds.
sections.takeaway: A green schedule is not proof of acceptable quality or risk.

sections.title: Eight of ten tasks is not necessarily 80% delivered
sections.explanation: Equal card counts can hide unequal work. Here the eight closed minor tasks represent only 40% of planned effort, while two testing tasks represent 60%. Even effort weighting is only a defined progress method; do not imply that a count or effort share proves accepted value.

items.label: Eight minor tasks
items.detail: Together account for 40% of planned effort in the example.

items.label: Two testing tasks
items.detail: Together account for the remaining 60%, with material acceptance risk.

sections.caption: Synthetic lesson weighting. The bars are planned-effort shares, not measured completion or earned-value claims.
sections.takeaway: State the progress method and verify accepted work before reporting a percentage.

sections.title: Put the decision above the attachments
sections.explanation: The sponsor should not have to reconstruct a decision from a board, budget and risk register. State what is needed, by when, which options are feasible and what happens if no decision is made. Link the evidence so the summary stays concise and auditable.

items.label: What changed?
items.detail: Baseline versus current forecast, cause and consequence.

items.label: What are the options?
items.detail: Move the pilot or defer optional reminders; protect mandatory checks.

items.label: Who decides by when?
items.detail: Named authority and an explicit date/trigger.

items.label: Where is the evidence?
items.detail: Versioned cost, schedule and risk references support the request.

sections.caption: Illustrative sponsor-brief structure. The actual decision date and authority must be supplied in the learner’s own case.
sections.takeaway: A useful report asks for action, not reassurance.

checkpoint.question: If eight minor tasks close but high-risk testing remains, is 80% a defensible completion claim?
checkpoint.answer: Not from task count alone. Use an agreed method and accepted evidence. In this example those eight tasks represent only 40% of planned effort, not proven value completion.

m6-t2.introduction: Prepare a meeting around a decision, explore the interests behind positions and leave an accurate durable record. A recommendation stays a recommendation until the proper authority decides.

sections.title: Invite the roles needed for the decision
sections.explanation: A decision-centred agenda states the question, options, evidence and necessary authority before the meeting. Include relevant expertise and accessible ways to contribute. If an essential approver is absent, record a recommendation rather than inventing a decision.

items.label: Define the question
items.detail: What decision must this meeting enable?

items.label: Prepare the evidence
items.detail: Concise options, impacts and pre-reading with a review window.

items.label: Bring the right roles
items.detail: Authority, expertise and affected voices; not every stakeholder by default.

items.label: Timebox and close
items.detail: Read back decisions, unresolved questions and next actions.

sections.caption: Conceptual meeting design, not a required extra ceremony or a record of an actual approval.
sections.takeaway: Attendance is not evidence that a decision was authorised.

sections.title: Look behind the position to the need
sections.explanation: “An extra week” and “the date cannot move” are positions. The underlying needs may be qualified testing and a safe event workflow. Explore scope and staffing alternatives while keeping mandatory privacy and safety outside the bargaining zone.

items.label: Vendor position → interest
items.detail: Extra week → access to a qualified tester and feasible support.

items.label: College position → interest
items.detail: Fixed event → safe core booking available at the right time.

items.label: Options → authority
items.detail: Defer reminders, move work or add qualified capacity only with proper approval.

sections.caption: Illustrative interest-based negotiation. It does not authorise contract, budget or safety concessions.
sections.takeaway: Preserve mandatory controls while comparing flexible options.

sections.title: Separate the decision from the remaining action
sections.explanation: A durable minute records what was approved, why, by whom and which version changes. An unresolved support concern still needs an owner and a date. A correction window improves accuracy; silence is not approval where explicit authorisation is required.

items.label: Decision record
items.detail: Illustrative sponsor choice: defer reminders and retain core safety testing.

items.label: Rationale and version
items.detail: Show the evidence, authority and the baseline revision reference.

items.label: Open action
items.detail: Vendor support concern remains visible with an owner and due date.

sections.caption: Synthetic meeting example from the lesson. The decision must be labelled simulated in a classroom portfolio.
sections.takeaway: Minutes are a decision/action record, not a verbatim transcript.

checkpoint.question: Does “no one replied to the minutes” prove a required sponsor approval?
checkpoint.answer: No. If policy needs explicit approval, silence cannot replace it. Keep the approval status pending and follow the agreed route.

m6-t3.introduction: Separate coordination from authorisation, test how scoring changes with weights and carry benefit ownership beyond handover. A ranking is not an investment decision.

sections.title: Different groupings answer different control questions
sections.explanation: A project delivers a bounded change; a programme coordinates related work for combined benefits; a portfolio supports strategic investment and shared-capacity choices. The PMO can supply standards and visibility without necessarily holding approval authority.

items.label: Project
items.detail: Bounded pilot with scope, acceptance and handover.

items.label: Programme
items.detail: Related changes coordinated to realise benefits together.

items.label: Portfolio
items.detail: Investments compared for strategy, constraints and capacity.

items.label: PMO support
items.detail: Definitions, reconciled reporting and governance according to its mandate.

sections.caption: Conceptual governance comparison. A job title or spreadsheet ownership does not establish budget authority.
sections.takeaway: Confirm the actual decision mandate rather than assuming it.

sections.title: A ranking can reverse when weights change
sections.explanation: The weighted total depends on the agreed preferences. At equal weights B leads, but increasing strategic-fit weight reverses the result. Show that sensitivity with capacity, evidence quality and mandatory conditions so that a score does not masquerade as an objective verdict.
sections.caption: Synthetic two-proposal sensitivity example from the lesson. Each bar is an alternative weighting result, not a quantity to add.
sections.takeaway: A high score cannot create missing capacity or waive a mandatory obligation.

sections.title: Keep the benefit review alive after project closure
sections.explanation: The receiving operation is often best placed to measure adoption and service outcomes. Give the benefit a baseline, target, definition, owner and review date; then identify influences that could affect the result. Do not count the same staff-hour saving in two initiatives.

items.label: Define the benefit
items.detail: Baseline, target and a measurable operational change.

items.label: Assign operational ownership
items.detail: Name who can observe adoption and service effects.

items.label: Measure after handover
items.detail: Collect comparable evidence at a planned review.

items.label: Review and adjust
items.detail: Separate measured results, forecasts and external influences.

sections.caption: Conceptual benefits-management loop. A delivered system or forecast is not evidence of realised savings.
sections.takeaway: A benefit needs an operational owner after the temporary team leaves.

checkpoint.question: Why does Project B’s 3.5 not automatically authorise it?
checkpoint.answer: It is a synthetic score under one weighting. Check sensitivity, mandatory conditions, funding and shared capacity; the authorised decision-maker still decides.

m6-pb4.introduction: Assemble a decision pack whose forecasts, versions and definitions reconcile. The visuals show the ₹40,000 EAC without replacing the ₹35,000 baseline or inventing a universal RAG policy.

sections.title: Show the gap before recommending the response
sections.explanation: The approved reference stays visible alongside the current forecast. A sponsor also needs the two-working-day schedule exception and the pending support decision. The cost snapshot and schedule delay are separate evidence, not values to combine into one arbitrary score.

items.label: Approved baseline
items.detail: Retained as the control reference.

items.label: Current EAC
items.detail: Actual ₹18,000 + current ETC ₹22,000 = ₹40,000.

sections.caption: Synthetic PB4 cost comparison: forecast overrun ₹5,000. The separate two-working-day delay needs a dated schedule explanation.
sections.takeaway: Make the variance visible instead of changing the reference to hide it.

sections.title: Freeze the reporting cut-off and source versions
sections.explanation: A weekly pack is credible when its figures use the same cut-off and documented versions. Keep the original cost snapshot and schedule reference, label any scenario changes and carry known gaps as owned actions. Do not imply the PMO has authorised its own proposal.

items.label: Cost source
items.detail: Baseline ₹35,000; AC ₹18,000; current ETC ₹22,000.

items.label: Schedule source
items.detail: Baseline versus forecast; explain the two-working-day exception.

items.label: Decision source
items.detail: Support request, options, named authority and pending/approved status.

items.label: Evidence index
items.detail: File, version, purpose and claim supported; safe public copy.

sections.caption: Synthetic PB4 inputs, separate from any task-duration-derived cost estimate. No live supplier decision is implied.
sections.takeaway: Reconcile provenance and definitions before polishing a summary.

sections.title: PB4: reserve time to verify and revise
sections.explanation: The classroom block is not all build time. Use the reproduction checkpoint to trace the headline result to source values, then retain the peer comment and correction. The final recommendation should follow the revised evidence, not the first attractive draft.

items.label: Frame and inspect
items.detail: Read the brief, boundaries and source fixtures.

items.label: Build required artefacts
items.detail: Create the linked outputs for this block.

items.label: Reproduce and review
items.detail: Check calculations, definitions and decisions.

items.label: Peer review and revise
items.detail: Keep the comment and the response.

items.label: Recommendation and AI statement
items.detail: Explain the decision and assistance transparently.

sections.caption: Published synthetic classroom allocation for PB4: 20 + 80 + 35 + 30 + 15 = 180 minutes. This is learner work time, not the delivery schedule’s working days.
sections.takeaway: A checked second version is more valuable than an unchecked first draft.

sections.title: One page should lead to the right evidence
sections.explanation: The headline report is the front door, not the whole analysis. Link each variance and decision to a checked working source. Portfolio recommendations also need sensitivity, capacity and a benefit owner so that ranking does not masquerade as approval.

items.label: Status summary
items.detail: Baseline, forecast, variance and defined RAG thresholds.

items.label: Reconciliation
items.detail: Cost formula plus schedule exception and evidence links.

items.label: Decision request
items.detail: Top risks/issues, options, recommendation, owner and deadline.

items.label: Governance record
items.detail: Agenda and minutes separate recommendations from decisions.

items.label: Portfolio and benefits
items.detail: Three proposals, sensitivity check and pilot benefit owner.

sections.caption: Conceptual map of PB4’s unchanged submission list. External marking and institutional authority remain separate from the platform.
sections.takeaway: A sponsor should find the required decision without opening every task record.

sections.title: Same cost formula, separate status dimensions
sections.explanation: EAC is actual cost plus the fresh remaining estimate, not the baseline remainder or EV added to AC. Whether a two-day delay is amber depends on the pre-agreed rule. A critical quality issue may have a different status and must remain visible.

items.label: Schedule status
items.detail: Two-day delay is amber only under the relevant agreed thresholds.

items.label: Quality and risk status
items.detail: Keep mandatory defects and material risk explicit; do not average away red.

sections.caption: Synthetic PB4 checks. The illustration does not establish institutional RAG thresholds or assert that a decision is approved.
sections.takeaway: A reconciled pack can be uncomfortable and still be professionally correct.

checkpoint.question: Does a two-day forecast delay always mean amber?
checkpoint.answer: No. Amber applies only if the pre-agreed schedule policy says so. Quality and risk can carry different statuses; the baseline must remain unchanged.

sections.title: Seven marks reward evidence and judgement
sections.explanation: Use the published rubric to inspect the work, not to invent new requirements. Correct arithmetic needs traceable inputs, professional judgement includes safeguards and authority, and clarity includes an evidence trail and reflection. The diagram does not award or upload marks.

items.label: Correctness and reproducibility
items.detail: Show the method, source values and a manual check.

items.label: Judgement and safeguards
items.detail: Make limits, provenance, authority and safe sharing explicit.

items.label: Clarity, evidence and reflection
items.detail: Keep the files navigable and explain the correction.

sections.caption: Illustrative display of the unchanged PB4 rubric: 3 + 2 + 2 = 7. Four blocks contribute 28 overall; external facilitator marking remains required.
sections.takeaway: Appearance alone cannot earn credit for an unsupported claim.

sections.title: Test the recommendation’s sensitivity and provenance
sections.explanation: Ask a peer to reproduce the forecast and locate its source date. Then change one portfolio weight to see whether the recommendation reverses. A high-ranked proposal still needs funding, capacity and authority; the benefit owner must be able to measure after handover.

items.label: Reconcile
items.detail: Do the summary and working file both use the current ETC?

items.label: Challenge status
items.detail: Were thresholds agreed before seeing this week’s result?

items.label: Test sensitivity
items.detail: Could weights or shared capacity reverse the portfolio choice?

items.label: Check the decision
items.detail: Are authority, deadline and no-decision consequence visible?

sections.caption: Conceptual PB4 peer-review aid. No real investment or benefit approval is implied.
sections.takeaway: A transparent uncertainty can be more useful than a precise-looking ranking.

sections.title: Disclose assistance and keep responsibility
sections.explanation: For the PMO decision pack, assistance can support drafting or checking, but it cannot create evidence that never existed. Complete the statement even if the answer is “none”. Keep only synthetic inputs in public tools and make your own verification visible.

items.label: Disclose use
items.detail: Tool or none, task assisted, and synthetic inputs shared.

items.label: Record your choices
items.detail: Suggestions accepted, changed or rejected, with your own contribution.

items.label: Verify independently
items.detail: Reconcile AC + current ETC, verify the delay basis and thresholds, and check portfolio weights and simulated approval labels.

items.label: Respect assessment boundaries
items.detail: Do not infer final-exam permission from project-tool permission.

sections.caption: Conceptual project AI-use workflow. It does not fabricate approvals, interviews, sources, business results or personal experience.
sections.takeaway: The learner remains responsible for the final numbers, claims and safeguards.

sections.title: Can the sponsor find the decision in thirty seconds?
sections.explanation: Use the optional peer test to improve information hierarchy. Ask the reviewer to identify the decision, deadline and consequence without coaching. If they cannot, simplify the summary while retaining links to the underlying facts and limitations.

items.label: Show the summary
items.detail: Let the peer act as sponsor without extra explanation.

items.label: Ask three questions
items.detail: What decision, by when, and what happens without it?

items.label: Revise the hierarchy
items.detail: Promote the decision and reduce detail that hides it.

items.label: Preserve the trail
items.detail: Keep versions and source links intact after editing.

sections.caption: Illustrative optional thirty-second usability check from PB4. It is not a new grading condition.
sections.takeaway: Clarity means faster access to the decision, not fewer safeguards.
